Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 53, verses 1–11 (part 1 of 2):

(p-104) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
Tafsir of Surat al-Najm (The Star).
It is Meccan by the consensus of the exegetes (al-mutawwilin). It is the first surah which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proclaimed and recited aloud in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) while the polytheists were listening. In it he prostrated, and the believers, the polytheists, the jinn and mankind prostrated with him, except Abu Lahab, who raised a handful of dust to his forehead and said: "This is enough for me." The occasion of this surah was that the polytheists said that Muhammad (ﷺ) was inventing the Qur'an and fabricating its statements, so the surah was revealed in response to that.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿By the star when it sets, your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred, nor does he speak from desire. It is nothing but revelation revealed. One mighty in power has taught him, one of strength, and he stood firm, while he was on the highest horizon. Then he drew near and descended, and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer. So He revealed to His servant what He revealed. The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾

Allah the Exalted swears by this created thing (al-makhluq) to honour it and to draw attention to it, so that it becomes a lesson (i'tibar) in it, until the lesson in it leads to the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted. Al-Zahrawi said: the meaning is "and by the Lord of the star," but this is awkward with the wording of the verse. The exegetes differed in specifying the star by which Allah swears. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Farra' and Mundhir ibn Sa'id, who clarified it, said: it is the whole of the Qur'an when it was sent down, for it is related that the Qur'an was sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ) in "nujum" (stars), that is, in determined measures at certain times. According to this interpretation, "hawa" (fell) means "nazala" (descended). But this "hawa" is still a stretch and does violence to the language. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 75], and the disagreement over it is like the disagreement over that.

Al-Hasan, Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna and others said: "al-najm" here is a noun of genus (ism jins); they meant the stars when they set. Those who held this view differed over the meaning of "hawa". The majority of exegetes said: "hawa" means setting (li-l-ghurub), and this is what comes first to mind from the speech of the Arabs. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: "hawa" means when they are scattered (inkidar) on the Day of Resurrection, and so it has the same meaning as His saying: ﴿And when the stars are scattered﴾ [al-Infitar: 2]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said in the book of al-Tha'labi: "hawa" means falling swiftly in pursuit of the 'ifriyya, which are the meteors of the devils. This view is supported by the language. All the interpretations of "hawa" are admissible and all are strong. As evidence for "al-najm" as a noun of genus, there is the verse of al-Ra'i:

"So they spent the night counting the star in a pot of ghee, quickly eaten by the hands of diners, its fat solid."

He describes a clarified fat; "al-mustahira" is the cooking-pot in which it is cooked, so said al-Zajjaj; al-Rummani said: it is pure fat when it has melted.

Mujahid and Sufyan said: the "najm" in the oath of the verse is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), and its setting with the dawn is its "hawiy". The Arabs do not say "al-najm" without qualification except for the Pleiades, and from this is the saying of the Arabs:

"The star rose at evening, so the herdsman sought a cloak; the star rose at morning, so the herdsman sought a sheepskin (shukayya)."

According to this view, "hawa" may mean setting and may mean falling. In the language, "hawa" means: tearing through the air, its aim being downward, or its end, even if he did not intend it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"My son fell from the edge of a mountain, so his foot and his hand slipped."

And the saying of a poet:

"Indeed the speech of a man out of its place is like arrows that fall with their heads missing."

And the saying of Zuhayr:

"...... falling like a bucket whose rope has released it."

(p-107) From it also is their saying of locusts: "al-hawi", and from it: "hawa al-'iqab" (the eagle swooped).

The oath falls upon His saying: ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾. "Dalal" (straying) is always without the person's intention towards it, while "ghayy" is something as if you acquire it deliberately and desire it. Allah the Exalted negated for His Prophet (ﷺ) that he had strayed on this path which Allah had made him follow. And Allah the Exalted affirmed in Surat [al-Duha] that he had been astray before prophethood in comparison with his state of guidance after it.

His saying: ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾ means that Muhammad (ﷺ) does not speak from his own desire, that is, by his whim and his lust. Some scholars said: the meaning is that the Qur'an, which was sent down, does not speak from whim and lust, and Allah attributed the speech to it in the sense that it is understood from it, as He said: ﴿This is Our Book which speaks against you with truth﴾ [al-Jathiya: 29], and He attributed the verb to the Qur'an though no mention of it had preceded, because the meaning indicates it. His saying: ﴿It is nothing but revelation revealed﴾ is intended to refer to the Qur'an by unanimous agreement. "Wahy" (revelation) is the casting of meaning in concealment; this expression covers the angel, inspiration, indication, and everything in which the meanings of revelation are preserved. The pronoun in His saying "taught him" (allamahu) may refer to the Qur'an, but the more apparent view is that it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). As for the teacher, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn 'Abbas said: it is Jibril (peace be upon him), that is, he taught Muhammad the Qur'an. Al-Hasan said: the teacher, the one of mighty power, is Allah the Exalted, and "al-quwa" is the plural of "quwwa" (strength); according to this, it applies to Jibril (peace be upon him) in a firmly established way, and this is supported by His saying: ﴿Possessor of power, established in the presence of the Lord of the Throne﴾ [al-Takwir: 20]. "Dhu mirra" means: possessor of strength, as said by Qatada, Ibn Zayd and al-Rabi', and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Charity is not lawful for the rich nor for one who has sound strength (dhi mirra sawiyy)." The root of "mirra" is from the "maraʾir" of a rope, which is its twisting and the firm making of its work, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays: (p-108)

"...... every strongly twisted cord was tightened at Yadhbul."

Some of those who said that the one "of mirra" is Jibril said: the meaning of "dhu mirra" is: possessor of a good form; others said: rather, it means: possessor of a tall, good body. All of this is weak.

"Istawa" is attributed to Allah the Exalted in the saying of al-Hasan, who said that He is the one described by His saying "mighty in power". Likewise His saying: ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ is a description of Allah the Exalted, in the sense that His greatness, His power and His dominion are what we perceive to be on the highest horizon, and the meaning comes close to His saying: ﴿The Most Merciful established Himself on the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]. Whoever said that the one described by His saying "mighty in power" is Jibril (peace be upon him) said that "istawa" is attributed to Jibril (peace be upon him). They then differed after that. Al-Rabi' and al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: Jibril (peace be upon him) stood firm in the air while he was then on the highest horizon, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him at Hira', having filled the horizon, with six hundred wings. Then he drew near to Muhammad (ﷺ) until he was at a distance of two bow-lengths. Likewise, according to this view, he is the one seen in the "second descent" in his great form, having six hundred wings, at the Lote-tree (al-Sidra). Al-Tabari and al-Farra' said: the meaning is: Jibril (peace be upon him) stood firm, and His saying: ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), whose mention preceded in the pronoun in "his knowledge (ilmihi)". In this interpretation there is coordination (al-'atf) upon a raised pronoun without emphasis, which the grammarians consider objectionable. al-Farra' cited as evidence for his view: (p-109)

"Do you not see that the firm wood (al-nab') hardens its stalk, while the brittle castor-plant does not stand firm?"

It may also be reversed, so that "istawa" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ) and "while he was on the highest horizon" refers to Jibril (peace be upon him). As for "al-a'la" (the highest), in my view it is the top of the head and what happened with it. al-Hasan and Qatada said: it is the horizon of the rising of the sun; but this specification has no evidence.

People differed as to whom the words "then he drew near and descended" refer. The majority said: it refers to Jibril (peace be upon him), that is, he drew near to Muhammad (ﷺ) at Hira'. Ibn 'Abbas and Anas, may Allah be pleased with them, in the hadith of the Isra' indicate that it refers to Allah the Exalted. Then the interpreters differed: Mujahid said: the drawing near was to Jibril (peace be upon him); some said: it was to Muhammad (ﷺ), and "fa-tadalla" (and descended) according to this view has an elided genitive (hadhf mudaf), that is: his authority, his revelation and his decree drew near; and motion and these attributes are negated with respect to Allah, blessed and exalted.

The correct view in my opinion is that everything in these verses concerns Jibril (peace be upon him), by the evidence of His saying: ﴿And he saw him in another descent﴾ [al-Najm: 13], for that requires an earlier descent. Nor has it ever been related that Muhammad saw his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, before the night of the Isra', although the seeing of the heart is not precluded in any way.

(p-110) "Dana" is more general than "tadalla", so by His saying "fa-tadalla" Allah explains the form of the drawing near, however it was. "Qab" means: measure. Qatada and others said: it means from the end of the bow to its other end. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: from the bowstring to the wood in the middle of the bow at the grip. Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' al-Yamani read: "wa-kana qay qawsayn", and the meaning is close to "qab". From this word is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "The space of one of your bows in the way of Allah is better than the world and what is in it." In another hadith: "The space of one of your bows in Paradise." His saying: "aw adna" means: according to the measure of human perception, that is, if one of you had seen it he would say: "two bows or nearer." Abu Razin said: it is not this bow, but the measure of two cubits or nearer. al-Zahrawi related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that "al-qaws" in this verse is a cubit by which lengths are measured; al-Tha'labi mentioned it, and said it is from the dialect of the Hijaz.

His saying: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: the meaning is: Allah the Exalted revealed to His servant Muhammad (ﷺ) what He revealed. Some scholars said: the meaning is: Allah the Exalted revealed to His servant Jibril (peace be upon him) what He revealed. In His saying "what He revealed" there is ambiguity by way of magnification and exaltation, and what is known from it is the obligation of prayer (salat). Al-Hasan said: the meaning is: Jibril revealed to the servant of Allah, Muhammad, upon both of them be prayer and peace, what He revealed, similar to the first in ambiguity. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: Jibril revealed to the servant of Allah what Allah revealed to Jibril, upon both of them be prayer and peace.

The words of the Most High: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾. The majority of the readers (al-qurra', the transmitters of the recitations) read "kadhaba" with a light (unshaddated) dhal, meaning: the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not deny what he saw; rather, it affirmed it and verified it through sight. Here "kadhaba" is transitive.

Among the people of ta'wil (interpretive exegesis), including Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) and Abu Salih, some said: Muhammad (ﷺ) saw Allah the Exalted with his heart. Others among the interpreters said: what he saw with his eyes, his heart did not deny; rather, it affirmed and verified it. It is also possible that the implied sense is: "in what he saw."

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), as narrated from him, along with 'Ikrimah and Ka'b al-Ahbar, said: Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, with the eyes of his head. Al-Zahrawi expounds this statement on their behalf.

'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) rejected this and said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about these verses, and he said to me: 'It is Jibril in all of them.'"

Al-Hasan said the meaning is: what he saw of the decreed things of Allah the Exalted and His dominion (malakut).

"Abu Dharr asked the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Did you see your Lord?' He said: 'It is light; how could I see Him?'" This is the view of the majority. The hadith of 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) from the Prophet (ﷺ) is decisive against every interpretation of the wording, because the statements of others are merely derived from the words of the Qur'an.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), as narrated from him by Hisham, read "ma kadhdhaba" with a shaddah on the dhal. This is also the reading of Abu Raja', Abu Ja'far, Qatada, al-Jahdari and Khalid. Its meaning is clear in light of some of what we have already said.

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Allah the Exalted divided speech and sight between Musa and Muhammad (may blessings and peace be upon them both): Musa spoke with Allah twice, and Muhammad saw Him twice.

'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "My hair stood on end from hearing this, and I said: ﴿No vision can grasp Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103]..." 

She, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada and the majority of scholars held that the one seen was Jibril (peace be upon him) on both occasions: on the earth, and at Sidrat al-Muntaha on the night of the Isra'. This has already been mentioned in Surat [al-Isra'], and it is well known both on earth and at Sidrat al-Muntaha on the night of the Isra', and it is well known in the books of the Sahihs (the authentic collections of hadith).

The readers Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir recited this entire surah with a fath (open vowel) at the ends of its verses. In the narration of Abu Bakr, 'Asim inclined "ra'a" (imalah). Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recited between fath and kasr. Hamza and al-Kisa'i inclined all of the surah's words. Abu 'Amr, as narrated from him by Abu 'Ubayd, inclined "al-A'la" and "tadalla".

According to this interpretation, "hawa" (fell) means "nazala" (descended). But this "hawa" is still a stretch and does violence to the language. Al-Hasan, Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna and others said: "al-najm" here is a noun of genus (ism jins); they meant the stars when they set. Those who held this view differed over the meaning of "hawa". The majority of exegetes said: "hawa" means setting (li-l-ghurub), and this is what comes first to mind from the speech of the Arabs. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: "hawa" means when they are scattered (inkidar) on the Day of Resurrection, and so it has the same meaning as His saying: ﴿And when the stars are scattered﴾ [al-Infitar: 2]. "So they spent the night counting the star in a pot of ghee, quickly eaten by the hands of diners, its fat solid."

He describes a clarified fat; "al-mustahira" is the cooking-pot in which it is cooked, so said al-Zajjaj; al-Rummani said: it is pure fat when it has melted.

Mujahid and Sufyan said: the "najm" in the oath of the verse is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), and its setting with the dawn is its "hawiy". The Arabs do not say "al-najm" without qualification except for the Pleiades, and from this is the saying of the Arabs:

"The star rose at evening, so the herdsman sought a cloak; the star rose at morning, so the herdsman sought a sheepskin (shukayya)."

"My son fell from the edge of a mountain, so his foot and his hand slipped."

And the saying of a poet:

"Indeed the speech of a man out of its place is like arrows that fall with their heads missing."

And the saying of Zuhayr:

"...... falling like a bucket whose rope has released it."

The oath falls upon His saying: ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾. Allah the Exalted negated for His Prophet (ﷺ) that he had strayed on this path which Allah had made him follow. Some of those who said that the one "of mirra" is Jibril said: the meaning of "dhu mirra" is: possessor of a good form; others said: rather, it means: possessor of a tall, good body. All of this is weak.

(p-116) The words of the Exalted: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ ﴿And Manat, the third, the other?﴾ ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ ﴿That, then, is an unjust division.﴾ ﴿They are only names you and your fathers have named; Allah has sent down no authority for them. They follow only conjecture and what their souls desire, though guidance has already come to them from their Lord.﴾ ﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾ ﴿But to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession will avail nothing, except after Allah grants permission to whom He wills and approves.﴾

The Exalted said: ﴿Have you considered﴾ is addressed to the Quraysh, and it is the seeing of the eye (ru'yat al-'ayn), because He refers to visible bodies. Had it been "ra'a" in the sense of asking for a judgement (istiftā'), it would not have taken a second object.

When He had finished mentioning the greatness of Allah and His power, He said, by way of rebuke: Consider these idols, their worthlessness, and how far they are from this power and these sublime attributes.

"Al-Lat" is the name of an idol that the Arabs used to venerate. Abu 'Ubayda and others said it was in the Ka'ba. Qatada (p-116) said it was in al-Ta'if. Ibn Zayd said it was at a palm tree near the market of 'Ukaz. Qatada's view is the more probable, supported by the verse of the poet:

؎ Thaqif fled to their al-Lat, returning as a defeated, losing one.

The "tā'" in "al-Lat" is the lām al-fi'l (the root letter, i.e. the radical of the verb), like the "bā'" in "bāb." Some said it is the tā' al-ta'nīth (the feminine marker), but morphological analysis (taṣrīf) prevents this. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Abu Salih read "al-Lātu" with a doubled tā'. They said this idol was a rock, and beside it was a man from Bihz who would knead the pilgrims' sawīq (parched-grain porridge) on that rock and serve the idols. When he died, they worshipped the rock that was beside him, out of reverence for that man, and named it after him. This reading is also narrated from Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir.

"Al-'Uzza" is a white rock, which the Arabs also worshipped and venerated, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Mujahid said it was small trees that were worshipped; then, when they decayed, its status passed to a rock. "'Uzzā" is the feminine of "'azīz," like kubrā and 'uẓmā. These idols were venerated and worshipped; each tribe would have one idol that it venerated, and every Arab who came would venerate it along with the venerating of its inhabitants. Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar said that al-'Uzza and Manat were in the Ka'ba. Ibn Zayd said al-'Uzza was in al-Ta'if, and Qatada said it was at Nakhla. As for Manat, it was at al-Mushallal, from Qadid, which lies between Makkah and Madina. It was the greatest of these idols in status and the most worshipped. The Aws and the Khazraj would make the pilgrimage (ihlāl) to it. For this reason Allah said: ﴿And Manat, the third, the other﴾, emphasizing it with these two attributes, just as you say: "I saw so-and-so and so-and-so," then mention a third who is greater than them and say: "and the other so-and-so, whose matter and affair is such-and-such." The words "ākhar" and "ukhrā" are used to describe the third of the counted items, and this is explicit in the verse. From this is the saying of Rabi'a ibn Mukdam:

؎ And indeed I paired the two of them with another, a third.

This is the correct interpretation of the words of the poet:

؎ I made for her two sticks of nasham and another from thumāma.

(p-117) Ibn Kathir alone read "wa-Munā'a" with a hamza and a long vowel, and this is a dialectal form of it. The first (Manāt) is more well known and is the reading of the people. From it is the saying of Jarir:

؎ Azyad of Manāt, threatening with the son of Taym: consider where your threat has led you astray.

Allah made the disbelievers stop at these idols and at what they said about them, because they used to say: "They are the daughters of Allah." It is as though He said: Have you considered these idols, and your saying that they are the daughters of Allah? ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ That is: is the kind that is praised and loved present with you, while the kind that is blamed and disliked by you is, by your claim, for Him? Then He said, in denunciation: ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾, that is, crooked (i'wajā'), as Mujahid said. It was also said that "ḍīzā" means unjust (jā'ira), as Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said. Sufyan said it means deficient (manqūṣa), and Ibn Zayd said it means contrary (mukhālifa). The Arabs say: "ḍizttuhu ḥaqqahu, aḍīzuhu," meaning: I withheld from him his right and wronged him in it. "Ḍīzā" comes from this morphological pattern. Its original form is fu'lā with a dammah on the fā', "ḍūzā," because that is the regular analogy, since no adjective of the form fi'lā with a kasrah on the fā' is found. This is what Sibawayh and others said. If that is so, then the original is "ḍūzā," but they put a kasrah on its first letter as the first letter of "'ayn" and "bayḍ" was given a kasrah, seeking lightness (takhfīf), since the kasrah and the yā' are lighter than the ḍammah and the wāw, as they said: "buyūt" and "'iṣiyy," though in origin it is fa'ūl with a ḍammah on the fā'. The Arabs say: "ḍizttuhu adūzuhu," so by this morphology it should have been "ḍūzā" as fu'lā. All of this is open to question. Ibn Kathir read "ḍi'zā" with a hamza, as a verbal noun (maṣdar) like dhikrā, while the majority read it without a hamza.

This is what the verse requires, although the wording is general enough to include him.

"Al-ākhira and al-ūlā" are the two abodes, meaning that all their affairs, in ownership, power, and under His authority, belong to Him.

His words: ﴿And how many an angel...﴾ — the verse... is a refutation of the Quraysh in their saying: "The idols are our intercessors." ؎ Thaqif fled to their al-Lat, returning as a defeated, losing one.

؎ And indeed I paired the two of them with another, a third.

The words of the Most High:

Allah the Most High informed that they have no knowledge of this, and that it is merely assumptions on their part for which they have no proof. These are matters of realities, in which assumptions are of no benefit. As for rulings (ahkam) and their outward aspects, assumed matters (al-maznunat) suffice in them.

Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided.﴾ ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil according to what they did and recompense those who did good with the best.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 53, verses 32–38:

﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the grave immoralities, except for minor lapses. Indeed, your Lord is vast in forgiveness. He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth and when you were embryos in your mothers' wombs. So do not claim purity for yourselves; He knows best who is mindful of Him.﴾ ﴿Have you considered the one who turned away,﴾ ﴿and gave a little and then held back?﴾ ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he can see?﴾ ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses,﴾ ﴿and of Abraham, who fulfilled his duty?﴾ ﴿That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another.﴾

His words, exalted is He: "Those who" is a qualifier (na't) of the "those who" mentioned before it. "Yajtanibuna" (avoid) means: they leave aside, keep at a distance. The majority of reciters and people read "kaba'ira al-ithm" (the major sins). Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-A'mash, 'Isa, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "kabira al-ithm" in the singular, which is used with the meaning of the plural. This is like His saying: ﴿Then we have no intercessors﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 100] ﴿nor a warm friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 101], and like His saying: ﴿and what excellent companions they are﴾ [al-Nisa': 69].

People have differed concerning the "kaba'ir" (major sins): what are they? The majority held that they are the seven destructive sins (al-muwabiqat) that are mentioned in the hadiths. The discussion of mentioning them and the differences in the hadiths about them has already passed in surah [al-Nisa']. The precise statement on the major sins is that they are every disobedience for which a legal penalty (hadd) is prescribed in this world and for which a fire is threatened in the Hereafter, or a curse or something similar specific to it. Therefore their number is great. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, when he was asked, "Are they seven?", said: "They are nearer to seventy than to seven." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "The 'major sin' here is meant to be disbelief (kufr)." The "fawahish" (grave immoralities) are the disobediences already mentioned. His words, "except for minor lapses" (al-lamam), is an exception that may be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil). If you consider it a disconnected exception (munqati'), that is also permissible.

People have differed concerning the meaning of "al-lamam". Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is what they committed of polytheism and disobedience in the time of ignorance before Islam. al-Tha'labi related from Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Thabit, Zayd ibn Aslam and his father that the cause of the verse was that the disbelievers said to the Muslims: "You used to do our deeds yesterday," and so the verse was revealed. It is like His saying: ﴿and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and others said: its meaning is: except what they committed of disobediences, a slip or a lapse, not persisted in, then they repent from it. al-Tabari reported from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan that he said: "It is a momentary lapse into fornication, theft or drinking wine, and then one does not return to it." This is like the previous view, so it seems that this interpretation requires leniency towards people in including them in the promise of the best reward, since it is common for believers to fall into disobediences. On this basis they recited (the poem), and the Prophet (ﷺ) quoted it:

"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much, and which servant of Yours does not commit lapses?"

Abu Hurayra, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi and others said: "al-lamam" is the small sins that lie between the two limits of this world and the Hereafter, which are those for which there is no legal penalty and no specific threat mentioned for them. It is only called "small" in comparison with other sins; otherwise, in relation to the one who forbids them, they are all major sins. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah has written for the son of Adam his share of adultery, inevitably. The adultery of the eye is the gaze, the adultery of the tongue is speech, and the private part either confirms that or denies it. If the private part advances, then he is an adulterer; otherwise it is a lamam." It is also narrated that this verse was revealed concerning Nabhan the date-seller. People do not escape from committing these minor sins, and yet with that, they have the best reward if they avoid those which are major in themselves. The scholars agreed on this view, and many inclined to it. al-Tabari reported from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "al-lamam is what is less than polytheism." However, in my view this is not sound from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr. al-Mahdawi reported from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sha'bi: "al-lamam is what is less than adultery." Nifthawayh said: "al-lamam is what is not habitual." al-Rummani said: "al-lamam is the intention to commit a sin and inner speaking about it without actually doing it." al-Tha'labi related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that it is whatever passes through the heart, and that is the "lamma" (passing impulse) of Satan. al-Zahrawi said: "It has also been said that al-lamam is a sudden glance (nazrat al-fuja'a)," and al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl also said this. Then, after this, Allah, exalted is He, gave assurance with His words: ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness.﴾

His words, exalted is He: ﴿He knows you best﴾ — the verse. It is related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that it was revealed concerning a people of the Jews who used to exalt themselves, and who would say to a child who died among them: "This one is a friend of Allah, exalted is He," and similar baseless claims. So the verse was revealed concerning them, and then in meaning it is general to all mankind. al-Tha'labi related from al-Kalbi and Muqatil that it was revealed concerning a people among the believers who boasted of their deeds. His words, exalted is He: ﴿He knows you best﴾. Makki ibn Abi Talib said in al-Mushkil: "Its meaning is: He is knowing of you." Most of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: "Rather, it is superlative in absolute terms, that is, He is more knowing than all those who exist collectively." The governing element of "idh" (when) is "a'lam" (knows best). Some grammarians said: the governing element is an implied verb whose estimate is: "Remember when." The first meaning is clearer, because its estimate is: if His knowledge has encompassed you while you are in these states, and concealment has befallen you, then it is more fitting that it should encompass you while you are heedless and committing sins.

"Al-insha' min al-ard" (the production from the earth) is intended to mean the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, and it may also be intended to mean the production of nourishment. "Ajinna" is the plural of "janin" (embryo). His words, exalted is He: ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾: its apparent meaning is a prohibition against anyone praising himself, and it may be a prohibition against some people praising others. If that is the case, then it prohibits praise for the sake of reputation, and extolling for worldly gain, and asserting purity with certainty. From this is the hadith about 'Uthman ibn Maz'un at his death. As for the praise of a leader or model of someone so that he may be followed, or so that people may be encouraged towards good, it is permissible. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) praised some of his companions, Abu Bakr and others, may Allah be pleased with them. Likewise, the attestation of witnesses in rights is permissible because of the need for it. The root of "purity" (tazkiyya) is only piety, and Allah, exalted is He, knows the piety of people better than you do.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Have you considered the one who turned away﴾ — the verse. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and others said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi. He had heard the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ), sat with him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) admonished him. He drew close to Islam, and the Prophet (ﷺ) hoped for him. Then a man among the polytheists rebuked him and said: "Will you abandon the religion of your fathers? Return to your religion and remain upon it, and I will bear for you everything you fear in the Hereafter, but on condition that you give me such-and-such amount of wealth." al-Walid ibn al-Mughira agreed to that, and turned back from what he had been inclined to of Islam, and went far astray. He gave that wealth to that man, then withheld and stinted. So the verse was revealed concerning him. al-Tha'labi mentioned from some people that it was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, in a story that occurred between him and 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh. All of that, in my view, is false, and 'Uthman is exempt from such things. al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il. On this view, His words, exalted is He: ﴿gave a little and then held back﴾ refers to wealth. Muqatil ibn Hayyan, in the book of al-Tha'labi, said the meaning is: "He gave something of himself, a little, in his nearness to faith, then he held back what he had given." This is clear from the wording, whereas the other requires a report. "Tawalla" means: he turned his back and turned away, and what is intended is: from the command of Allah, exalted is He. "Akda" means: his giving ceased. It is likened to a digger in the earth: when he reaches a hard stone (kudya), which is the hardest part of the ground, he stops and his digging ends. Similarly, "ajbala" is said of a digger who reaches a rock (jabal). Then it is said of one whose work has ceased: "akda" and "ajbala."

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he can see?﴾ means: does he know from the unseen that whoever bears the sins of another, the one who bears on his behalf benefits from that? Thus, through this knowledge, he sees the truth and has insight into it. Or is he ignorant and has not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses, which is the Torah, and in the scriptures of Abraham, which are books that were sent down to him from heaven, that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another? That is, no one carrying a load shall carry the load of another, and each person is only held to account for his own sins. Since he was ignorant of this, he fell into giving his wealth to the one who said to him: "I will bear the consequences of the Hereafter on your behalf."

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿the one who fulfilled (wafa)﴾. Fulfilled what, and who is the one fulfilled? Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: before Abraham, peace be upon him, they used to seize a relative (wali) for another relative in killing and the like. Abraham, peace be upon him, fulfilled this and conveyed the ruling that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said, and so did al-Rabi': it means obedience to Allah, exalted is He, in sacrificing his son, peace be upon them both. 'Ikrima said: he fulfilled these ten verses, beginning with "that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" and what follows it. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and 'Ikrima said: he fulfilled what was obligatory upon him of acts of obedience in their proper form, and the branches of faith and Islam were perfected for him, so Allah, exalted is He, granted him freedom from the Fire. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: he fulfilled the laws of Islam, thirty parts. Abu Umama, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), said: he fulfilled four prayers each day. The strongest of all these is the general view that it refers to all acts of obedience which complete the religion of Islam. It is reported that these were not prescribed upon anyone in complete form, so that he fulfilled them, except Abraham and Muhammad (ﷺ). Among the evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [al-Baqara: 124].

Ibn Jubayr, Abu Malik and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "wafa" with a light fa'. The disagreement concerning what he fulfilled is like the disagreement concerning what was fulfilled for him according to the first reading that we explained. The reading is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Abu Umama recited it.

"Al-wizr" is the burden. The feminine form "al-wazira" is used either because the intended meaning is the soul (nafs), or because it intends intensification, like "'allama" and "nassaba," and what follows their pattern. The "anna" in His words, glorified is He: ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear...﴾ "alla tazir" is the light form of the heavy (anna), and its estimate is: "annahu la tazir." The separation between it and the verb is permissible if the verb remains in the nominative, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that there will be among you the sick and others﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] and similar. And "an" is in a position of nominative or genitive, both are governed.

This is like His saying: ﴿Then we have no intercessors﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 100] ﴿nor a warm friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 101], and like His saying: ﴿and what excellent companions they are﴾ [al-Nisa': 69].

People have differed concerning the "kaba'ir" (major sins): what are they? The majority held that they are the seven destructive sins (al-muwabiqat) that are mentioned in the hadiths. The discussion of mentioning them and the differences in the hadiths about them has already passed in surah [al-Nisa']. The precise statement on the major sins is that they are every disobedience for which a legal penalty (hadd) is prescribed in this world and for which a fire is threatened in the Hereafter, or a curse or something similar specific to it. Therefore their number is great. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, when he was asked, "Are they seven?", said: "They are nearer to seventy than to seven." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "The 'major sin' here is meant to be disbelief (kufr)." The "fawahish" (grave immoralities) are the disobediences already mentioned. His words, "except for minor lapses" (al-lamam), is an exception that may be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil). If you consider it a disconnected exception (munqati'), that is also permissible.

People have differed concerning the meaning of "al-lamam". Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is what they committed of polytheism and disobedience in the time of ignorance before Islam. al-Tha'labi related from Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Thabit, Zayd ibn Aslam and his father that the cause of the verse was that the disbelievers said to the Muslims: "You used to do our deeds yesterday," and so the verse was revealed. It is like His saying: ﴿and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and others said: its meaning is: except what they committed of disobediences, a slip or a lapse, not persisted in, then they repent from it. al-Tabari reported from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan that he said: "It is a momentary lapse into fornication, theft or drinking wine, and then one does not return to it." This is like the previous view, so it seems that this interpretation requires leniency towards people in including them in the promise of the best reward, since it is common for believers to fall into disobediences. On this basis they recited (the poem), and the Prophet (ﷺ) quoted it:

"If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much, and which servant of Yours does not commit lapses?"

Abu Hurayra, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi and others said: "al-lamam" is the small sins that lie between the two limits of this world and the Hereafter, which are those for which there is no legal penalty and no specific threat mentioned for them. It is only called "small" in comparison with other sins; otherwise, in relation to the one who forbids them, they are all major sins. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah has written for the son of Adam his share of adultery, inevitably. The adultery of the eye is the gaze, the adultery of the tongue is speech, and the private part either confirms that or denies it. If the private part advances, then he is an adulterer; otherwise it is a lamam." It is also narrated that this verse was revealed concerning Nabhan the date-seller. People do not escape from committing these minor sins, and yet with that, they have the best reward if they avoid those which are major in themselves. The scholars agreed on this view, and many inclined to it. al-Tabari reported from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "al-lamam is what is less than polytheism." However, in my view this is not sound from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr. al-Mahdawi reported from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sha'bi: "al-lamam is what is less than adultery." Nifthawayh said: "al-lamam is what is not habitual." al-Rummani said: "al-lamam is the intention to commit a sin and inner speaking about it without actually doing it." al-Tha'labi related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that it is whatever passes through the heart, and that is the "lamma" (passing impulse) of Satan. al-Zahrawi said: "It has also been said that al-lamam is a sudden glance (nazrat al-fuja'a)," and al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl also said this. Then, after this, Allah, exalted is He, gave assurance with His words: ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness.﴾

His words, exalted is He: ﴿He knows you best﴾ — the verse. It is related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that it was revealed concerning a people of the Jews who used to exalt themselves, and who would say to a child who died among them: "This one is a friend of Allah, exalted is He," and similar baseless claims. So the verse was revealed concerning them, and then in meaning it is general to all mankind. al-Tha'labi related from al-Kalbi and Muqatil that it was revealed concerning a people among the believers who boasted of their deeds. His words, exalted is He: ﴿He knows you best﴾. Makki ibn Abi Talib said in al-Mushkil: "Its meaning is: He is knowing of you." Most of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: "Rather, it is superlative in absolute terms, that is, He is more knowing than all those who exist collectively." The governing element of "idh" (when) is "a'lam" (knows best). Some grammarians said: the governing element is an implied verb whose estimate is: "Remember when." The first meaning is clearer, because its estimate is: if His knowledge has encompassed you while you are in these states, and concealment has befallen you, then it is more fitting that it should encompass you while you are heedless and committing sins.

"Al-insha' min al-ard" (the production from the earth) is intended to mean the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, and it may also be intended to mean the production of nourishment. "Ajinna" is the plural of "janin" (embryo). His words, exalted is He: ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾: its apparent meaning is a prohibition against anyone praising himself, and it may be a prohibition against some people praising others. If that is the case, then it prohibits praise for the sake of reputation, and extolling for worldly gain, and asserting purity with certainty. From this is the hadith about 'Uthman ibn Maz'un at his death. As for the praise of a leader or model of someone so that he may be followed, or so that people may be encouraged towards good, it is permissible. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) praised some of his companions, Abu Bakr and others, may Allah be pleased with them. Likewise, the attestation of witnesses in rights is permissible because of the need for it. The root of "purity" (tazkiyya) is only piety, and Allah, exalted is He, knows the piety of people better than you do.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Have you considered the one who turned away﴾ — the verse. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and others said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi. He had heard the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ), sat with him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) admonished him. He drew close to Islam, and the Prophet (ﷺ) hoped for him. Then a man among the polytheists rebuked him and said: "Will you abandon the religion of your fathers? Return to your religion and remain upon it, and I will bear for you everything you fear in the Hereafter, but on condition that you give me such-and-such amount of wealth." al-Walid ibn al-Mughira agreed to that, and turned back from what he had been inclined to of Islam, and went far astray. He gave that wealth to that man, then withheld and stinted. So the verse was revealed concerning him. al-Tha'labi mentioned from some people that it was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, in a story that occurred between him and 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh. All of that, in my view, is false, and 'Uthman is exempt from such things. al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il. On this view, His words, exalted is He: ﴿gave a little and then held back﴾ refers to wealth. Muqatil ibn Hayyan, in the book of al-Tha'labi, said the meaning is: "He gave something of himself, a little, in his nearness to faith, then he held back what he had given." This is clear from the wording, whereas the other requires a report. "Tawalla" means: he turned his back and turned away, and what is intended is: from the command of Allah, exalted is He. "Akda" means: his giving ceased. It is likened to a digger in the earth: when he reaches a hard stone (kudya), which is the hardest part of the ground, he stops and his digging ends. Similarly, "ajbala" is said of a digger who reaches a rock (jabal). Then it is said of one whose work has ceased: "akda" and "ajbala."

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he can see?﴾ means: does he know from the unseen that whoever bears the sins of another, the one who bears on his behalf benefits from that? Thus, through this knowledge, he sees the truth and has insight into it. Or is he ignorant and has not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses, which is the Torah, and in the scriptures of Abraham, which are books that were sent down to him from heaven, that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another? That is, no one carrying a load shall carry the load of another, and each person is only held to account for his own sins. Since he was ignorant of this, he fell into giving his wealth to the one who said to him: "I will bear the consequences of the Hereafter on your behalf."

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿the one who fulfilled (wafa)﴾. Fulfilled what, and who is the one fulfilled? Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: before Abraham, peace be upon him, they used to seize a relative (wali) for another relative in killing and the like. Abraham, peace be upon him, fulfilled this and conveyed the ruling that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said, and so did al-Rabi': it means obedience to Allah, exalted is He, in sacrificing his son, peace be upon them both. 'Ikrima said: he fulfilled these ten verses, beginning with "that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" and what follows it. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and 'Ikrima said: he fulfilled what was obligatory upon him of acts of obedience in their proper form, and the branches of faith and Islam were perfected for him, so Allah, exalted is He, granted him freedom from the Fire. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: he fulfilled the laws of Islam, thirty parts. Abu Umama, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), said: he fulfilled four prayers each day. The strongest of all these is the general view that it refers to all acts of obedience which complete the religion of Islam. It is reported that these were not prescribed upon anyone in complete form, so that he fulfilled them, except Abraham and Muhammad (ﷺ). Among the evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [al-Baqara: 124].

Ibn Jubayr, Abu Malik and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "wafa" with a light fa'. The disagreement concerning what he fulfilled is like the disagreement concerning what was fulfilled for him according to the first reading that we explained. The reading is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Abu Umama recited it.

"Al-wizr" is the burden. The feminine form "al-wazira" is used either because the intended meaning is the soul (nafs), or because it intends intensification, like "'allama" and "nassaba," and what follows their pattern. The "anna" in His words, glorified is He: ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear...﴾ "alla tazir" is the light form of the heavy (anna), and its estimate is: "annahu la tazir." The separation between it and the verb is permissible if the verb remains in the nominative, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that there will be among you the sick and others﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] and similar. And "an" is in a position of nominative or genitive, both are governed.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 53, verses 39–51:**

[p. 127] His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And that there is not for man except what he strives for.﴾ ﴿And that his striving will be seen.﴾ ﴿Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense.﴾ ﴿And that to your Lord is the finality.﴾ ﴿And that it is He who causes laughter and causes weeping.﴾ ﴿And that it is He who causes death and gives life.﴾ ﴿And that He created the pairs, the male and the female,﴾ ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted.﴾ ﴿And that upon Him is the second creation.﴾ ﴿And that it is He who enriches and suffices.﴾ ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius.﴾ ﴿And that He destroyed ʿAd, the first,﴾ ﴿and Thamud, and spared none.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, "*wa-an laysa*" (and that there is not), and His saying after that, "*wa-anna*" and "*wa-annahu*" (and that), are all coordinated with the implied "*an*" in His saying, "*allā taziru wāziratun wizra ukhrā*" (that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another). All of them are with an opening *alif* (*fatḥ*) in the recitation of the majority. Abū al-Samāl Quʿnab recited "*wa-inna ilā rabbika al-muntahā*" with a kasra on the hamza in it and in what follows it. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that His saying, "*wa-an laysa lil-insāni illā mā saʿā*," is abrogated (*mansūkh*) by His saying, "*wa-alladhīna āmanū wa-ittabaʿathum dhurriyyatuhum bi-īmānin alḥaqnā bihim dhurriyyatahum*" [al-Ṭūr: 21]. This, in my view, is not sound as attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, because it is a report that is not abrogated, and because the conditions of abrogation (*naskh*) are not present here. Except that the term "abrogation" may be used loosely, so that it is understood by the questioner.

ʿIkrima said: This ruling was for the people of Ibrahim and Musa, peace be upon them both. As for this Ummah, it has the striving of others as well. The evidence is the hadith of Saʿd ibn ʿUbada, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, will my mother receive a reward if I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes."

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: The "man" in this verse is the disbeliever. As for the believer, [p. 127] he has what he strove for and what others strove for on his behalf.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ṭāhir ibn al-Ḥusayn, the governor of Khurasan, asked al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl about this verse together with His saying, "*wa-llāhu yuḍāʿifu li-man yashāʾ*" [al-Baqara: 261]. He said to him: "It is not by justice except what one has strived for, and for him, by the grace of Allah, is what Allah wills." So ʿAbd Allah kissed al-Ḥusayn's head.

The majority said: the verse is *muḥkam* (firm, with a clear and unabrogated ruling). My own elucidation of this verse is that the core of the meaning lies in the *lām* in His saying, "*lil-insān*" (for man). When you establish what truly belongs to a person, such that one says of it "it is mine," you will find nothing but his striving. What comes afterward of mercy, through intercession, or the care of a righteous father or a righteous son, or the multiplying of good deeds, or being covered by grace and mercy, apart from all of this, does not belong to the human being in the strict sense, and he cannot say "it is mine, such and such," except by way of figurative extension and attachment to what is truly his.

Those who hold that no one acts on behalf of another after his death, neither with the body nor with wealth, have used this verse as evidence. Some scholars distinguished between the body and wealth. In my view, all of these are merits for the doer and good deeds that are credited to the one on whose behalf they are done. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded Saʿd, may Allah be pleased with him, to give charity on behalf of his mother.

"*Saʿy*" (striving) means earning.

His saying, "*yurā*" (will be seen): its subject is present, namely the Resurrection; that is, Allah sees it and whoever witnesses the matter. The presentation of deeds before everyone is an honor for the good-doers and a rebuke for the wrongdoers. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever publicizes (the faults of) his brother in what he dislikes, Allah will publicize him before all of His creation on the Day of Resurrection."

In His saying, "*thumma yujzāhu al-jazāʾ al-awfā*" (then he will be recompensed with the fullest recompense), there is a threat for the disbelievers and a promise for the believers.

"*Al-Muntahā*" (the finality): it may be that by it is meant the gathering and the return after death; it is a final point in relation to this world, though after it there is another final point, which is Paradise or Hell. It may also be that by *al-muntahā* is meant Paradise or Hell, in which case it is a final point absolutely. However, there is an elided *muḍāf* (a word understood) in the speech, that is: "to the punishment of your Lord or His mercy." Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Prophet ﷺ said concerning His saying, "*wa-anna [p. 128] ilā rabbika al-muntahā*": "Do not reflect upon the Lord." And Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the Lord is mentioned, then stop (reflecting)." Abū Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out one day to his companions and said: "What are you occupied with?" They said: "We are reflecting on the Creator, glorified and exalted is He." He, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "Reflect upon the creation, and do not reflect upon the Creator, for thought cannot encompass Him..." (the hadith).

He, exalted is He, mentioned laughter and weeping because they are two attributes that gather many kinds of people, since each one is a sign of joy and the other a sign of sorrow, in this world and in the Hereafter. So He drew attention to these two particular qualities which belong to man alone. Mujāhid said: The meaning is: He made the people of Paradise laugh and made the people of Hell weep. Al-Thaʿlabī related on this matter several figurative sayings, such as one who said: "He made the earth laugh with vegetation and made the sky weep with rain," and similar.

"*Amāta wa-aḥyā*" (He causes death and gives life) is clear. Al-Thaʿlabī related an opinion that He gives life by faith and causes death by disbelief.

"*Al-zawjayn*" (the pairs) in this verse means the mated human beings: male and female, and whatever resembles them among animals. The hermaphrodite is distinguishable, and necessarily belongs to one of the two categories.

"*Nuṭfa*" (drop) in language means a portion of water, whether small or large. Here it is intended to mean the male seed.

His saying, "*tumnā*" (when it is emitted), may be from your saying "*amnā al-rajul*" (the man emitted *manī*, semen), when *manī* came out of him. It may also be from your saying "*manna Allāhu al-shayʾ*" (Allah measured/determined the thing), when He created it; as if He said: when it is formed and measured.

"*Al-nashʾa al-ukhrā*" (the second creation) is the restoration of bodies for the gathering after they have decayed in their composition. The people recited "*al-nashʾa*" with a sukūn on the shīn and with hamza and short vowel (*qaṣr*). Abū ʿAmr and al-Aʿraj recited "*al-nashāʾa*" with a long vowel (*madd*).

"*Aqnā*" means: he earned. You say *qanaytu al-māl*, meaning I earned the wealth. Then after that it was transitive with the hamza, and transitive with doubling. From this is the saying of the poet:

*How many a rich man has been struck by fate in his wealth, and how many a poor man has become wealthy after destitution.*

The commentators expressed the meaning of "*aqnā*" in various phrases. Some said: its meaning is: he acquired what one keeps as property (*yuqtanā*). Mujāhid said: its meaning is: he was pleased and made rich. Ḥaḍramī said: its meaning is: he made himself rich, and "*aqnā*" made His servants poor and in need of Him. Al-Akhfash said: "*aghnā*" means: made poor. These are phrases that the word does not require, and the correct meaning according to the language is: He gave what is kept as property. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "*aqnā*" means: made content (*aqnaʿa*).

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Contentment is the best possession, and wealth is a passing accident. So how excellent is the wisdom of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

"*Al-Shiʿrā*" is a star in the sky. Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: it is Marzam al-Jawzāʾ (the companion of Orion). There are two Sirii: one is al-Ghumayṣāʾ, and the other is al-ʿUbūr, because it crossed the Milky Way. The Khuzāʿa were among those who worshipped this Sirius, and among them was Abū Kabsha; al-Zahrāwī and al-Thaʿlabī mentioned him, and his name was ʿAbd al-Shiʿrā. For this reason it was singled out for mention; that is: He is the Lord of this worshipped one which you have.

"*ʿĀd*" is the people of Hud. Scholars differed on the meaning of describing them as "*al-ūlā*" (the first). Ibn Zayd and the majority said: this is because they were at the beginning of time and its ancient past, so they are the first in relation to the later nations. Al-Ṭabarī said: they were called "the first" because there was later another ʿĀd, a tribe, which was in Mecca with the ʿAmālīq, and they were the Banū Luqaym ibn Hazāl. The first opinion is clearer, because the latter has not been authenticated. Al-Mubarrad said: the last ʿĀd is Thamūd, and the evidence is the verse of Zuhayr:

*...like the red one of ʿĀd; then you suckle, then you wean.*

al-Zahrāwī mentioned it. It was also said: the last are the tyrants. Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī recited "*ʿĀdan*" with tanwīn and "*al-ūlā*" with hamza. Nāfiʿ, as related from him, recited "*ʿĀdan al-ūlā*" with the removal of the tanwīn and the hamza, and this is like the recitation of the one who recited "*aḥadun Allāh*" (Qurʾan 112:1, with the tanwīn elided), and like the saying of the poet:

*...and none remembers Allah except a little.*

Some recited "*ʿĀdun al-ūlā*," and the pronunciation is "*ʿĀdanni al-ūlā*": the sukūn of the nūn of tanwīn and the sukūn of the lām of the definite article met, so the nūn was vowelled with a kasra to resolve the meeting of two sukūns. There is no difference between this and the recitation of the majority except the dropping of the hamza. Nāfiʿ also, and Abū ʿAmr, recited with connection and assimilation: "*ʿĀdan li-wulā*," with the nūn assimilated into the lām and the vowel of the hamza transferred to the lām. Abū ʿUthmān al-Māzinī and al-Mubarrad criticized this recitation and said: this transfer does not remove the lām from the state of sukūn, and the right of the alif of connection is that it remain, as the Arabs say when the hamza is transferred from their saying "*al-aḥmar*" (the red): they say "*al-ḥmar jāʾa*" (the red one came). Likewise it would be said here: "*ʿĀdan lil-ūlā*." Abū ʿAlī said: the recitation is valid. Moreover, among the Arabs there are those who say "*laḥmar jāʾa*," so the alif is elided with the transfer, and the vowel of the lām is counted and not regarded as in the state of sukūn. Nāfiʿ, as related from him, recited "*ʿĀdan al-lu'lā*" with a hamza on "*al-lu'lā*," hamzating the waw. The basis of this is that there was no barrier between the waw and the ḍamma which would prevent the hamza, so he hamzated it as the ḍamma-waw is hamzated, and likewise the one who recited "*ʿalā suʾqihi*" (on his shank). And as the poet said:

*...the two fires were more beloved to me, Mūsā...*

and this is a dialect. The majority recited "*wa-Thamūdan*" in the accusative, coordinated with "*ʿĀdan*." ʿĀṣim, al-Ḥasan and ʿIṣma recited "*wa-Thamūdu*" without tanwīn. In the codex of Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, it is written without an alif after the dāl.

His saying, "*fa-mā abqā*" (and spared none): its apparent meaning is: "he spared none of them." Some interpreted it as: "he did not leave among them a single eye that blinks." Al-Ḥajjāj said this when he heard the statement of one who said that the Thaqīf were from Thamūd. He denied it and said: Allah, may He be exalted, said: "*wa-Thamūda fa-mā abqā*" (and Thamūd, and He spared none), and those people say: "some of them remained."

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 53, verses 39–51:**

[p. 127] His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And that there is not for man except what he strives for.﴾ ﴿And that his striving will be seen.﴾ ﴿Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense.﴾ ﴿And that to your Lord is the finality.﴾ ﴿And that it is He who causes laughter and causes weeping.﴾ ﴿And that it is He who causes death and gives life.﴾ ﴿And that He created the pairs, the male and the female,﴾ ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted.﴾ ﴿And that upon Him is the second creation.﴾ ﴿And that it is He who enriches and suffices.﴾ ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius.﴾ ﴿And that He destroyed ʿAd, the first,﴾ ﴿and Thamud, and spared none.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, "*wa-an laysa*" (and that there is not), and His saying after that, "*wa-anna*" and "*wa-annahu*" (and that), are all coordinated with the implied "*an*" in His saying, "*allā taziru wāziratun wizra ukhrā*" (that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another). All of them are with an opening *alif* (*fatḥ*) in the recitation of the majority. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that His saying, "*wa-an laysa lil-insāni illā mā saʿā*," is abrogated (*mansūkh*) by His saying, "*wa-alladhīna āmanū wa-ittabaʿathum dhurriyyatuhum bi-īmānin alḥaqnā bihim dhurriyyatahum*" [al-Ṭūr: 21]. This, in my view, is not sound as attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, because it is a report that is not abrogated, and because the conditions of abrogation (*naskh*) are not present here. Except that the term "abrogation" may be used loosely, so that it is understood by the questioner.

ʿIkrima said: This ruling was for the people of Ibrahim and Musa, peace be upon them both. As for this Ummah, it has the striving of others as well. It may also be from your saying "*manna Allāhu al-shayʾ*" (Allah measured/determined the thing), when He created it; as if He said: when it is formed and measured.

The people recited "*al-nashʾa*" with a sukūn on the shīn and with hamza and short vowel (*qaṣr*). Abū ʿAmr and al-Aʿraj recited "*al-nashāʾa*" with a long vowel (*madd*).

*How many a rich man has been struck by fate in his wealth, and how many a poor man has become wealthy after destitution.*

The commentators expressed the meaning of "*aqnā*" in various phrases. Some said: its meaning is: he acquired what one keeps as property (*yuqtanā*). Mujāhid said: its meaning is: he was pleased and made rich. Ḥaḍramī said: its meaning is: he made himself rich, and "*aqnā*" made His servants poor and in need of Him. Al-Akhfash said: "*aghnā*" means: made poor. These are phrases that the word does not require, and the correct meaning according to the language is: He gave what is kept as property. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "*aqnā*" means: made content (*aqnaʿa*).

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Contentment is the best possession, and wealth is a passing accident. So how excellent is the wisdom of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

For this reason it was singled out for mention; that is: He is the Lord of this worshipped one which you have.

*...and none remembers Allah except a little.*

*...the two fires were more beloved to me, Mūsā...*

Al-Ḥajjāj said this when he heard the statement of one who said that the Thaqīf were from Thamūd. He denied it and said: Allah, may He be exalted, said: "*wa-Thamūda fa-mā abqā*" (and Thamūd, and He spared none), and those people say: "some of them remained."

His saying, may He be exalted, "*wa-an laysa*" (and that there is not), and His saying after that, "*wa-anna*" and "*wa-annahu*" (and that), are all coordinated with the implied "*an*" in His saying, "*allā taziru wāziratun wizra ukhrā*" (that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another). All of them are with an opening *alif* (*fatḥ*) in the recitation of the majority. Abū al-Samāl Quʿnab recited "*wa-inna ilā rabbika al-muntahā*" with a kasra on the hamza in it and in what follows it. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that His saying, "*wa-an laysa lil-insāni illā mā saʿā*," is abrogated (*mansūkh*) by His saying, "*wa-alladhīna āmanū wa-ittabaʿathum dhurriyyatuhum bi-īmānin alḥaqnā bihim dhurriyyatahum*" [al-Ṭūr: 21]. This, in my view, is not sound as attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, because it is a report that is not abrogated, and because the conditions of abrogation (*naskh*) are not present here. Except that the term "abrogation" may be used loosely, so that it is understood by the questioner.

ʿIkrima said: This ruling was for the people of Ibrahim and Musa, peace be upon them both. As for this Ummah, it has the striving of others as well. The evidence is the hadith of Saʿd ibn ʿUbada, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, will my mother receive a reward if I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes."

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: The "man" in this verse is the disbeliever. As for the believer, [p. 127] he has what he strove for and what others strove for on his behalf.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ṭāhir ibn al-Ḥusayn, the governor of Khurasan, asked al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl about this verse together with His saying, "*wa-llāhu yuḍāʿifu li-man yashāʾ*" [al-Baqara: 261]. He said to him: "It is not by justice except what one has strived for, and for him, by the grace of Allah, is what Allah wills." So ʿAbd Allah kissed al-Ḥusayn's head.

The majority said: the verse is *muḥkam* (firm, with a clear and unabrogated ruling). My own elucidation of this verse is that the core of the meaning lies in the *lām* in His saying, "*lil-insān*" (for man). When you establish what truly belongs to a person, such that one says of it "it is mine," you will find nothing but his striving. What comes afterward of mercy, through intercession, or the care of a righteous father or a righteous son, or the multiplying of good deeds, or being covered by grace and mercy, apart from all of this, does not belong to the human being in the strict sense, and he cannot say "it is mine, such and such," except by way of figurative extension and attachment to what is truly his.

Those who hold that no one acts on behalf of another after his death, neither with the body nor with wealth, have used this verse as evidence. Some scholars distinguished between the body and wealth. In my view, all of these are merits for the doer and good deeds that are credited to the one on whose behalf they are done. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded Saʿd, may Allah be pleased with him, to give charity on behalf of his mother.

They said: "We are reflecting on the Creator, glorified and exalted is He." ﴿And the people of Noah before them; indeed, they were more unjust and more rebellious.﴾ ﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down.﴾ ﴿Then covered them with what covered them.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old.﴾ ﴿The Imminent Hour has drawn near.﴾ ﴿None besides God can avert it.﴾ ﴿Is it at this discourse that you marvel?﴾ ﴿And you laugh and do not weep?﴾ ﴿While you are heedless.﴾ ﴿So prostrate yourselves to God and worship.﴾

"The people of Noah" (qawma Nūḥin) is in the accusative, coordinated with "Thamūd" (in the preceding verses). His words, "from before" (min qablu), are because they were the first nation among the people of the earth to deny (their prophet), and Noah was the first of the messengers. He described them as "more unjust and more rebellious" (aẓlama wa-aṭghā) because they were the first to deny, without following anyone before them. Furthermore, they were extremely insolent, and Noah, peace be upon him, had prolonged his lifetime in calling them (to the truth). A man would come to him with his son and say: "I warn you against this man, for he is a liar. My father warned me against him, and he informed me that my grandfather had warned him against him." Thus their character continued on this for a thousand years less fifty years.

"The overturned cities" (al-mu'tafikah) refers, by the unanimous agreement (ijma', consensus of the scholars of Qur'anic exegesis) of the exegetes, to the town of the people of Lot, peace be upon him. The meaning of al-mu'tafikah is "the overturned," because it was overturned and then turned upside down. From the same root comes "al-ifk" (falsehood), because it is the reversal of truth into falsehood. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan recited "wal-mu'tafikāt" in the plural. The meaning of "ahwā" is that He threw them from a high air downward. This is what is narrated, that Gabriel, peace be upon him, uprooted them with his wing until he brought them near the sky, then they all descended, and then they were pursued with stones, which are what God, blessed and exalted, covered them with.

His words, "So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?" are addressed to the disbelieving human being, as if it were said to him: "This is God, who has these deeds, and He is your Creator, the One who bestows upon you all blessings. So in which of these do you doubt?" The word "tatamārā" means "you doubt," and Ya'qūb recited "rabbika tammārā" with a single, doubled tā'. Abū Mālik al-Ghifārī said that His words, "that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" (al-Najm: 38), up to His words "you dispute," are in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses, peace be upon them both.

His words, "This is a warner," may refer to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is the view of Qatādah, Abū Ja'far, and Muḥammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazī. It may also refer to the Qur'an, and this is the interpretation of some people. Abū Mālik said: the reference of "this warner" is to the reports about the nations that preceded. The word "nadhīr" may be an active participle form, and it may be a verbal noun. "Nudhur" is the plural of "nadhīr." He said "al-Ūlā" meaning that in rank, attributes, and status it is equal to those earlier ones. The more likely reading is that the reference is to Muhammad (ﷺ).

His words, "The Imminent Hour has drawn near," mean: "the approaching one has drawn near." "Al-Āzifah" is, by the unanimous agreement of the exegetes, a designation for the Resurrection. "Azifa" means "drew very near." Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

Youth has departed, and grey hair has come near,
and I see no successor to departed youth.

His words, "kāshifah," may be an attribute of a feminine noun, the implied meaning being "a state that removes," or "a calamity that removes," or "an intercession." Al-Rummānī said: or "a group." It may be a verbal noun, like "al-'āqibah" and "khā'innat al-a'yun." It may also mean "one who removes," with the ta' marking intensity, as in His words, "Do you see any remnant of them?" (al-Ḥāqqah: 8). As for the meaning of "kāshifah," al-Ṭabarī and al-Zajjāj said it derives from "unveiling the secret," meaning: there is none besides God who can unveil its time and know it. Al-Zahrāwī, on the authority of Mundhir ibn Sa'īd, said: it means removing and repelling harm, that is, none can remove its terror and its calamity. Ṭalḥah recited: "Laysa lahā mimmā tad'ūna min dūni Allāhi kāshifah, wa-hiya 'alā al-ẓālimīna sā'at al-ghāshiyah."

"This discourse" (al-ḥadīth) is the Qur'an. His words, "Is it...?" are a rebuke and a reproach. In the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ūd, may God be pleased with them both, the words are "ta'jabūna, taḍḥakūna" without the conjunction "wa." Al-Ḥasan recited "ta'jabūna, taḍḥakūna" with the tā' vowelled with a ḍammah in both, the jīm and ḥā' with a kasrah, and the conjunction omitted. His words, "and do not weep," encourage weeping upon hearing the Qur'an. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqāṣ, may God be pleased with him, narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, this Qur'an was revealed as a warning. So when you recite it, weep, and if you do not weep, then feign weeping." Al-Tha'labī mentioned it.

"Al-sāmid" is the playful, heedless one, and Ibn 'Abbās, may God be pleased with them both, and other exegetes interpreted it this way. A poet said:

It was said: "Stand up and look at them,
then leave aside your heedlessness."

"Samada" in the dialect of Ḥimyar means "he sang." All of these meanings are close to one another. Al-Ṭabarī related, on the authority of Abū Khālid al-Wālibī, who said: 'Alī, may God be pleased with him, came out to us while we were standing waiting for the prayer, and said: "Why do I see you heedless?"

(p-135) Abū Muḥammad al-Qāḍī, may God have mercy on him, said:

It seems that he saw them engaged in idle talk or the like, which he considered a kind of heedlessness. Ibrāhīm said: they used to dislike waiting standing for the imam to come out. And in a hadith: "When the prayer is established, do not stand until you see me."

Then God, exalted, commanded prostration and the worship of God, as a warning and a threat. Here there is a prostration according to many scholars, among them ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, and sound hadiths have been transmitted concerning it. Mālik, may God, exalted, have mercy on him, did not hold it (as obligatory). Zayd ibn Thābit, may God be pleased with him, said: "He recited it in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not prostrate."

The commentary on Surah [al-Najm] is complete, and praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.
