﴿And the people of Noah before them; indeed, they were more unjust and more rebellious.﴾ ﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down.﴾ ﴿Then covered them with what covered them.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old.﴾ ﴿The Imminent Hour has drawn near.﴾ ﴿None besides God can avert it.﴾ ﴿Is it at this discourse that you marvel?﴾ ﴿And you laugh and do not weep?﴾ ﴿While you are heedless.﴾ ﴿So prostrate yourselves to God and worship.﴾

"The people of Noah" (qawma Nūḥin) is in the accusative, coordinated with "Thamūd" (in the preceding verses). His words, "from before" (min qablu), are because they were the first nation among the people of the earth to deny (their prophet), and Noah was the first of the messengers. He described them as "more unjust and more rebellious" (aẓlama wa-aṭghā) because they were the first to deny, without following anyone before them. Furthermore, they were extremely insolent, and Noah, peace be upon him, had prolonged his lifetime in calling them (to the truth). A man would come to him with his son and say: "I warn you against this man, for he is a liar. My father warned me against him, and he informed me that my grandfather had warned him against him." Thus their character continued on this for a thousand years less fifty years.

"The overturned cities" (al-mu'tafikah) refers, by the unanimous agreement (ijma', consensus of the scholars of Qur'anic exegesis) of the exegetes, to the town of the people of Lot, peace be upon him. The meaning of al-mu'tafikah is "the overturned," because it was overturned and then turned upside down. From the same root comes "al-ifk" (falsehood), because it is the reversal of truth into falsehood. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan recited "wal-mu'tafikāt" in the plural. The meaning of "ahwā" is that He threw them from a high air downward. This is what is narrated, that Gabriel, peace be upon him, uprooted them with his wing until he brought them near the sky, then they all descended, and then they were pursued with stones, which are what God, blessed and exalted, covered them with.

His words, "So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?" are addressed to the disbelieving human being, as if it were said to him: "This is God, who has these deeds, and He is your Creator, the One who bestows upon you all blessings. So in which of these do you doubt?" The word "tatamārā" means "you doubt," and Ya'qūb recited "rabbika tammārā" with a single, doubled tā'. Abū Mālik al-Ghifārī said that His words, "that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" (al-Najm: 38), up to His words "you dispute," are in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses, peace be upon them both.

His words, "This is a warner," may refer to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is the view of Qatādah, Abū Ja'far, and Muḥammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazī. It may also refer to the Qur'an, and this is the interpretation of some people. Abū Mālik said: the reference of "this warner" is to the reports about the nations that preceded. The word "nadhīr" may be an active participle form, and it may be a verbal noun. "Nudhur" is the plural of "nadhīr." He said "al-Ūlā" meaning that in rank, attributes, and status it is equal to those earlier ones. The more likely reading is that the reference is to Muhammad (ﷺ).

His words, "The Imminent Hour has drawn near," mean: "the approaching one has drawn near." "Al-Āzifah" is, by the unanimous agreement of the exegetes, a designation for the Resurrection. "Azifa" means "drew very near." Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

Youth has departed, and grey hair has come near,
and I see no successor to departed youth.

His words, "kāshifah," may be an attribute of a feminine noun, the implied meaning being "a state that removes," or "a calamity that removes," or "an intercession." Al-Rummānī said: or "a group." It may be a verbal noun, like "al-'āqibah" and "khā'innat al-a'yun." It may also mean "one who removes," with the ta' marking intensity, as in His words, "Do you see any remnant of them?" (al-Ḥāqqah: 8). As for the meaning of "kāshifah," al-Ṭabarī and al-Zajjāj said it derives from "unveiling the secret," meaning: there is none besides God who can unveil its time and know it. Al-Zahrāwī, on the authority of Mundhir ibn Sa'īd, said: it means removing and repelling harm, that is, none can remove its terror and its calamity. Ṭalḥah recited: "Laysa lahā mimmā tad'ūna min dūni Allāhi kāshifah, wa-hiya 'alā al-ẓālimīna sā'at al-ghāshiyah."

"This discourse" (al-ḥadīth) is the Qur'an. His words, "Is it...?" are a rebuke and a reproach. In the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ūd, may God be pleased with them both, the words are "ta'jabūna, taḍḥakūna" without the conjunction "wa." Al-Ḥasan recited "ta'jabūna, taḍḥakūna" with the tā' vowelled with a ḍammah in both, the jīm and ḥā' with a kasrah, and the conjunction omitted. His words, "and do not weep," encourage weeping upon hearing the Qur'an. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqāṣ, may God be pleased with him, narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, this Qur'an was revealed as a warning.
